concepts.def: Sound waves with a frequency higher than the upper limit of hearing for humans. Ultrasound is ordinary sound — a longitudinal wave needing a medium to travel through — and differs from audible sound only in having too high a frequency for the human ear to detect.
The highest frequency a human ear can detect. This specification gives the normal range of human hearing as 20 Hz to 20 kHz, so any sound wave with a frequency above about 20 000 Hz is ultrasound.

The surface where one material meets a different material, such as the surface between two tissues in the body, between metal and the air inside a crack, or between water and the sea bed. A boundary matters because the wave behaves differently on each side of it — it travels at a different speed and is absorbed by a different amount.

When ultrasound waves meet a boundary between two different media they are partially reflected: part of the wave is reflected back towards the detector and the rest carries on into the second medium. Because the reflection is only partial, the transmitted part can go on to reflect from deeper boundaries, so several boundaries can be found from a single pulse.

concepts.term: Finding a distance from the time of a reflection
concepts.def: The time taken for a reflection to reach a detector is used to work out how far away the boundary is. The distance the pulse travels is found from distance travelled = speed × time, using the speed of the wave in that medium. Because the pulse travels to the boundary and back, the distance to the boundary is half the distance the pulse has travelled.

A use of ultrasound in which a pulse is sent into the body and the reflections from the boundaries between different tissues are timed. Each boundary returns its reflection after a different time, so the depths of the boundaries can be found and built into an image of a structure that cannot be seen directly.

A use of ultrasound in which a pulse is sent into a manufactured object, such as a metal casting or a weld. A crack or void inside the object is a boundary between two different media, so it partially reflects the pulse; a reflection arriving earlier than the reflection from the far side shows that a flaw lies inside the object.

The transfer of energy from a wave to the material it is passing through, which reduces the energy the wave carries. Different types of wave are absorbed by different amounts in the same material, so a wave that is only weakly absorbed by a material can be used to explore what lies beyond it, while a strongly absorbed wave cannot.

concepts.term: Velocity of a wave in a medium
concepts.def: The speed at which a wave travels through a particular material. The same wave travels at different speeds in different solids and liquids, and different types of wave travel at different speeds through the same material. A change of speed at a boundary is what makes the boundary reflect part of the wave, and the speed must be known before a time can be turned into a distance.
Waves produced by earthquakes, which travel through the Earth and are picked up by detectors at the surface. They are of two kinds, P-waves and S-waves.
A longitudinal seismic wave. P-waves travel at different speeds through solids and liquids, so their speed changes when they cross from one part of the Earth's interior into another.
A transverse seismic wave. S-waves cannot travel through a liquid, so any region of the Earth's interior that S-waves fail to cross is evidence that the material there is liquid.

P-waves and S-waves provide evidence for the structure and size of the Earth's core. Detectors on the far side of the Earth from an earthquake receive no S-waves, which is evidence that part of the core is liquid; P-waves do arrive, but their speed changes where they cross into and out of the core, which alters the paths they follow and gives evidence about the size of the core and the structure within it.

The use of high frequency sound waves to detect objects in deep water and to measure water depth. A pulse is sent down from a ship, and the time for the echo to return from the sea bed or from an object is used to find how far away it is.

Structures that cannot be seen or reached — the inside of a body, a flaw inside a solid casting, the sea bed under deep water, the interior of the Earth. Waves reach these structures and return, so their differences in velocity, absorption and reflection allow the structures to be detected and explored indirectly. The study of seismic waves provided new evidence of exactly this kind, leading to discoveries about parts of the Earth which are not directly observable.

concepts.term: Detection and exploration using differences between waves
concepts.def: Detection means finding that something is there; exploration means working out its size, depth or structure. Both rest on the same three differences: a wave travelling at a different velocity in the hidden material is partially reflected at its boundary, the time of that reflection gives the distance, and a wave that is weakly absorbed by the material in between is the one that can reach the structure and return.

mcqs.q: Waves are sent down into the ground to search for a hidden layer of rock, in which the waves would travel at a different speed. What happens where the waves reach the top of the hidden layer?
options: The wave carries on at exactly the same speed as before
The whole wave is reflected and none carries on downwards
Part of the wave is reflected and part carries on downwards
The wave carries on but with a higher frequency than before
mcqs.explain: A change of velocity at a boundary between two different media produces a partial reflection. The reflected part returns to the detector and reveals the layer; the transmitted part continues and can reflect from deeper boundaries.

mcqs.q: In a survey, the waves pass easily through layer X but are strongly absorbed by layer Y, which lies beneath it. What effect does this have on the survey?
options: A strong reflection returns from layer Y because it absorbs waves
No reflections at all are received, even from the top of layer Y
Waves below layer Y speed up to make up for the energy they lost
Reflections from below layer Y are weak or missing at the detector
mcqs.explain: Absorption transfers the wave's energy to layer Y, so little energy reaches anything below it and little returns. A strongly absorbing layer hides whatever lies beneath it.

mcqs.q: Differences in which three properties, between different types of wave in solids and liquids, are used to detect and explore hidden structures?
options: Velocity, absorption and reflection
Frequency, absorption and reflection
Amplitude, absorption and reflection
Velocity, absorption and refraction
mcqs.explain: These are the three properties named in the specification, and each has a distinct role: velocity change creates the reflection, reflection returns the signal, and low absorption lets the wave reach the structure and come back.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly describes ultrasound waves?
options: Sound waves with a frequency above the upper limit of human hearing
Sound waves that are much louder than a human ear can safely hear
Electromagnetic waves used to make images of the inside of the body
Sound waves with a frequency below the lower limit of human hearing
mcqs.explain: This is the specification's definition. Ultrasound is sound; only its frequency puts it beyond what the ear can detect.

mcqs.q: An ultrasound pulse sent into the body meets three tissue boundaries one after another. Why can a reflection be received from all three?
options: The pulse is reflected in full at each boundary that it reaches
Only part of the pulse reflects at each boundary; the rest goes on
The pulse speeds up at each boundary, so it reaches them all
The pulse is absorbed at each boundary and then sent out again
mcqs.explain: Ultrasound is partially reflected at a boundary between two different media, so the transmitted part survives to reach and reflect from the next boundary.

mcqs.q: An ultrasound pulse is sent into a steel block to look for a crack. Ultrasound travels at 6000 m/s in the steel. A reflection from the crack is received 0.000 040 s after the pulse is sent. How far below the surface is the crack?
mcqs.explain: distance travelled = speed × time = 6000 × 0.000 040 = 0.24 m. The pulse travelled to the crack and back, so the crack is 0.24 ÷ 2 = 0.12 m below the surface.

mcqs.q: A pulse of ultrasound is sent into a steel casting. From one region a reflection returns much sooner than the reflection from the far side of the casting. What is the best conclusion?
options: A boundary such as a crack lies inside that region
The casting must be thicker in that region than elsewhere
The ultrasound was completely absorbed in that region
The ultrasound was completely reflected at the outer surface
mcqs.explain: An earlier reflection means a shorter distance travelled, so there is a boundary between two different media nearer the surface than the far side — a flaw inside the casting.

mcqs.q: Which statement explains how an ultrasound scan builds up an image of a structure inside the body?
options: Ultrasound is absorbed by bone, casting a shadow onto a film
Ultrasound is completely reflected by the first tissue it meets
Reflections from boundaries between tissues arrive at different times
Ultrasound is absorbed by the tissues and then re-emitted by them
mcqs.explain: Each boundary partially reflects the pulse, and the time each reflection takes to reach the detector gives the distance to that boundary, so the depths can be assembled into an image.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly describes P-waves and S-waves?
options: P-waves are transverse and S-waves are longitudinal
P-waves are longitudinal and S-waves are transverse
Both are longitudinal, like all waves in solid rock
Both carry the rock along with them as they travel
mcqs.explain: Exactly as the specification states: P-waves are longitudinal, seismic waves and S-waves are transverse, seismic waves.

mcqs.q: Which statement about seismic waves travelling through the Earth is correct?
options: Neither S-waves nor P-waves can travel through any liquid
S-waves can travel through any liquid, but P-waves cannot
S-waves cannot travel through a liquid, but P-waves can
P-waves travel at one fixed speed through solid and liquid
mcqs.explain: The specification states that S-waves cannot travel through a liquid; P-waves do travel through liquids, though at a different speed from in solids.

mcqs.q: After an earthquake, detectors on the far side of the Earth receive P-waves but no S-waves. What does this provide evidence for?
options: The core is a hollow space with no material inside it at all
S-waves are transverse, so they cannot travel through a solid
Part of the core is liquid, so S-waves cannot pass through it
The core is solid, and it absorbed the S-waves completely
mcqs.explain: S-waves cannot travel through a liquid, so their failure to arrive is evidence of a liquid region; the P-waves that do arrive show there is material there to travel through.

mcqs.q: How do P-waves provide evidence about the size of the Earth's core?
options: Their speed changes at the core boundary, bending their paths
They cannot enter the core, so a total shadow is produced
They travel at one steady speed everywhere inside the Earth
They become transverse waves once inside the liquid core
mcqs.explain: P-waves travel at different speeds through solids and liquids, so their speed changes where they enter and leave the core; the resulting paths and arrival points give evidence about how large the core is.

mcqs.q: A P-wave travels through solid rock. How does the rock move as the wave passes?
options: At right angles to the direction the wave travels
The rock itself is carried along with the wave
Parallel to the direction in which the wave travels
In circles around a point on the wave's path
mcqs.explain: P-waves are longitudinal, so the oscillations of the rock are parallel to the direction of energy transfer.

mcqs.q: Which statement about echo sounding is correct?
options: Radio pulses are used because they travel well through water
High frequency sound is used to find depth and locate objects
Light pulses are used because light travels fastest in water
Sound is used, but only the outward trip of the pulse is timed
mcqs.explain: Echo sounding, using high frequency sound waves, is used to detect objects in deep water and to measure water depth.

mcqs.q: A ship uses echo sounding to measure the depth of the sea. The speed of the sound waves in the sea water is 1500 m/s and the echo from the sea bed returns 0.80 s after the pulse is sent out. How deep is the water?
mcqs.explain: distance travelled = speed × time = 1500 × 0.80 = 1200 m. That is down and back, so the depth is 1200 ÷ 2 = 600 m.

mcqs.q: Echo sounding uses high frequency sound waves rather than light or radio waves. Why?
options: Light and radio pulses would work just as well at any depth
Sound travels faster through sea water than light does
Sound waves are the only waves that reflect off a sea bed
Water absorbs light and radio waves much more strongly than sound
mcqs.explain: This is a difference in absorption between types of wave. Only the sound pulse travels far enough through deep water and returns strongly enough to be detected.

mcqs.q: Why was the study of seismic waves so important for our knowledge of the Earth?
options: It confirmed what had already been seen by drilling to the core
It proved that the inside of the Earth cannot be studied at all
It allows the exact time of the next earthquake to be predicted
It gave new evidence about regions nobody can observe directly
mcqs.explain: The study of seismic waves provided new evidence that led to discoveries about parts of the Earth which are not directly observable.

mcqs.q: Measurements of seismic waves led scientists to conclude that part of the Earth's core is liquid. This conclusion is an example of scientists:
options: taking samples of the core from very deep mines and boreholes
using indirect evidence to reach a conclusion about a hidden region
guessing, because a hidden region cannot be studied by evidence
confirming an idea by observing the core region of the Earth directly
mcqs.explain: The waves themselves are measured at the surface; the structure they passed through is inferred from which waves arrive and when. That is indirect evidence, and it is how parts of the Earth that are not directly observable came to be known.
